Comments to the Authors:

We are sorry to say that, after consultation with the reviewers, we have decided that your work will not be considered further for publication by eLife.

There was overwhelming enthusiasm for the manuscript and agreement regarding the strengths of the paper by the reviewers. These include the timely and important question of the role of dopamine in aversion, as well as the experimental approach especially the variety of behavioural tasks used. The strengths have been expressed by the reviewers in their individual comments (see below). However, a number of concerns were raised that require substantial reframing (punishment vs. aversive stimulus) of the manuscript as well as additional data collection. Although the reviewers' individual comments are appended to the decision letter, I wanted to give a brief overview of the discussion that led to the decision. One of the key aspects of the paper is the idea that dopamine concentration should be modulated in a white noise intensity-specific manner. However, the behavioural evidence that the white could be discriminated at different intensities came using different parameters compared to the neurochemical experiment. It is paramount to show that given these parameters the animals can indeed discriminate the white intensities as this is key to the argument of whether dopamine tracks aversive prediction error. Relatedly, behavioural evidence of conditioning is needed in the context of the recordings. The influence of baseline choice and amplitude vs. duration of the signal on the data need to be explored further. A more specific concern regarding the lack of correspondence between Figure 2B trace and bar graphs. It was unclear to the reviewers how the trace data correspond to the bar graphs below the trace. The statistical methods and degrees of freedom were also unclear. While this is a short overview of some of the concerns that were flagged, it is not exhaustive, further concerns are noted in the individual reviews. The reviewers and editors felt that addressing these concerns is beyond the scope of a standard eLife revision. However, given the enthusiasm for the manuscript if you are able to well address each of the reviewers concerns, we would be willing reconsider the manuscript for publication at eLife as a new submission, with a point by point rebuttal to each concern.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Understanding the role of dopamine beyond reward and specifically in aversion is of fundamental importance. The paper set out to examine whether dopamine concentration in the nucleus accumbens tracks aversive prediction error as it does in reward. To do this, the authors used fast-scan cyclic voltammetry alongside a number of key behavioural manipulations that have been shown to provide conditions for detecting reward prediction error. The behavioral designs used are established and appropriate to the questions posed. While the aversive cue, a loud white noise, employed was not standard, the paper provides behavioural evidence for its effectiveness as an aversive outcome. Although a closer examination of the learning that underlies the task design is necessary. While the analyses of the neural signal are appropriate, some alternatives could be explored in order to better understand the profile of the dopamine signal during the behavioural tasks employed, including evaluation of baseline fluctuations. Relating dopamine concentration to aversive events to that seen to rewarding events will provide important insight into the role of dopamine in general and valence-specific learning mechanisms.

A thorough examination of accumbal dopamine concentration levels to a aversive event and its predictor using some of the key conditions under which a (reward) prediction error is reported. As a result of this thorough investigation the paper is a real tour de force. Some comments/concerns are outlined below.

Interpretation of the data.

The temporal window of DA. Across the experiments DA concentrations are examined during the predictive cue and the WN US and those concentrations are not in line with an error signal. This may be explained in terms of floor effects in the signal, but some aspects of the study argue against that – the signal during the CS for example. The authors have examined post WN period which shows a differential slope to an expected and an unexpected WN, which is in line with a PE account. A more complete analyses of the slope would be worth seeing. A justification for the slope is also necessary. Also, why not take the concentration during a specified post-WN period? The authors could analyze different temporal windows. Importantly, the post-WN period does suggest PE-like differences – most striking in Figure 2A, but potentially present in 2D, E,F.

The baseline subtraction. The authors have used a reasonable baseline, pre-CS period, of determining the change in DA release. However, it would be important to know if and how the baseline changes across the training sessions. It is unclear whether pre-cue baseline subtraction was done on a trial by trial basis or if one averaged baseline was calculated and then used to determine DA concentration change. This could influence the data.

Framing. While I really appreciated the framing of the approach within what has been reported for RPE, I wonder if failing to get the same profile is really conclusive regarding the absence of a PE signal using an aversive event. For example, a complete shift is not reported in all datasets that show a DA RPE signal. This can also be due to variability across animals. Further, it is possible that an aversive event may be tracked more categorically by DA , making the intensity and probability examinations less relevant for testing PE in the aversive case. Further, reduction in DA concentration may also be less sensitive to detecting these subtle changes. Is there anything in the data that can deal away with these points?

Methodology. It seems that a lot (all?) of the rats were ran across all experimental conditions. This raises concern over carry over effects.

Validation of the WN as aversive: The behavioural tasks do not include another auditory cue as a control comparison in the open field nor in the operant. The operant has different intensities of the WN, which helps matters as there is a difference between the 70dB and the 96dB. But it is unclear what the role of the WN is in these conditions. Is it just to show that it is aversive or that it can condition behaviour? I think there is evidence for the former but not the latter.

The manuscript should refer to the WN as an aversive stimulus, not punisher.

Please change all instances that refer to WN intensity (e.g. 70dB, 90dB, etc) as a volume. 'volume' is a colloquial way of referring to intensity and is therefore not appropriate in a scientific setting.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The manuscript by Goedhoop focuses on understanding the dopaminergic signals that are driven by aversive stimuli. The project uses fast scan cyclic voltammetry to directly record dopamine fluctuations in awake and behaving animals in response to a variety of task variables to parse their contribution to behavior across conditions.

There are a lot of strengths of this manuscript.

First – the use of white noise is innovative and powerful. The field often focuses on aversive footshocks, which are interesting but unique stimuli. The use of white noise allows for an aversive stimulus that is not painful and is not an electrical stimulus which is a significant advantage over previous studies.

Second – one issue in the field in general is that people focus on dopamine as an RPE encoder where dopamine in every context has been linked to RPE-like signaling. However, a shortcoming of previous work with direct dopaminergic recording approaches like voltammetry is that they are electrical in nature and thus, cannot record the response to the aversive stimulus (footshock) themselves. This is clearly and issue as the stimulus response is a critical variable to understand in order to make conclusions about whether something encodes "RPE" or not.

However, even with these strengths there are some significant weaknesses. These occur In both the conceptual presentation and the experimental execution and if addressed the manuscript would be much stronger.

1. Regarding the conceptual issues, the largest is the terminology used throughout the manuscript. One of the major issues in this manuscript is the definition of all aversive stimuli as punishers. A punishment has a specific definition that is incorrectly used here. A punisher is not defined by the valence of the stimulus, but rather the behavioral effect of that stimulus on future behavior. A punisher reduces rates of behavior – appetitive stimuli can also function as punishers. This is a huge problem and the wording in the manuscript should be changed to reflect this. This is incredibly problematic as it suggests that the findings are different than what they actually are on a conceptual level as they relate to what dopamine is doing.

2. There are many statements that are inherently problematic because of this mischaracterization of the behavior. For example: "this heterogeneity is reflected in dopamine responses to punishment throughout the striatum" is stated in the introduction; however, many of these studies are not punishment. Also, many people have suggested that dopamine controls motivational responses. In that case a "punisher" and "negative reinforcer" would show different dopaminergic signatures even though the maintaining stimulus is aversive in both cases. This is actually an important and overlooked aspect of this work and defining everything as a punisher makes it difficult to decipher what the data are showing and how that relates to the actual behavior of the animal.

3. These results can alternatively be explained by the novelty induced alterations of behavior in rodents. The literature has shown that rodents withhold consummatory behavior and novelty induces hyperactivity in rodents (e.g., Bardo et al.,1990; Psychopharmacol; but also see earlier paper from 1950s Berlyne 1955; Bindra and Spinner 1958; Welker 1959). The dopamine system is highly involved in both of these effects.

Regarding experimental issues:

1. The canonical unconditioned aversive response in rodents is freezing or immobility (e.g., Antoniadis and McDonald, 2001, Exp Brain Res). Here in Figure 1 and also in Figure 2C they show the whitenoise itself results in increase in locomotor activity. How do we know this is an aversive response comparable to other traditional aversive stimuli such as footshocks or tail pinches (which are shown to result in increase in NAc core dopamine release see Budygin et al., 2012; Mikhailova et al., 2019).

2. In Figure2A, the dopamine response to the white noise seems to be decreased. However, this is due to the baseline used to compute the white noise dopamine responses, which seems to shift lower due to the dopamine response to the antecedent cue. That is why the initial white noise dopamine response seems to be positive in Trial1 where the baseline is still above 0 but looks negative when the cue response becomes negative starting from Trial3. If the dopamine response to the white noise outcome were computed with a baseline of its own (1-2 sec before the WN outcome) that would result in a positive peak even in trials 11-30.

3. The authors claim that the decrease in dopamine response to the white noise during the first trial of aversive conditioning (Figure 2A) is an unconditioned response. However, there is an immediate positive peak after the white noise presentation on that trial, which lasts about 1 sec. How does the behavior map on to this timeline? Do rats move for the first second but then freeze for the remainder of the white noise presentation? At the very least a strong justification should be made for what is being normalized and if and how you can separate specific task components.

5. There are numerous studies where cues are paired with white noise as an aversive stimulus. It is important to determine if the predictive cue elicited a conditioned response. Without that how do you know the animals made the association? This is important to make conclusions about what the neural signal in response to these cues actually mean.

6. In response to the data with the white noise and different timing. Is this predicting the timing? Or the value of the outcome? These are not dissociable in this experiment and when you discuss timing this would be important to dissociate. This is a critical thing to parse as duration is in the title.

Overall this is an interesting manuscript however in order for it to be suitable for publication the authors should rephrase their terminology to accurately state what the stimuli are and how they relate to behavior as well as make sure to show that white noise does function as an aversive stimulus.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

In this study a talented group of neurochemists performed real-time measurements of dopamine concentration in behaving rats to investigate whether transient accumbal release events encode the value of aversive stimuli. Directly measuring dopamine release events rather than phasic bursts of putative dopamine neural activity is particularly important to determine how transient dopamine signals encode aversive events because recent evidence shows that terminal-terminal modulation influences behaviorally relevant patterns of release that do not necessarily coincide with changes in neural activity. The authors also incorporated an impressive systematic behavioral design and a unique aversive stimulus (i.e., white noise) to address this unresolved controversy. First, they determined that high decibel white noise produced a conditioned place aversion and punished food seeking. Then, by presenting comparable levels of white noise within a Pavlovian context, they found that dopamine release events were suppressed during the presentation an aversive stimulus and its conditioned predictor. They further report that the magnitude by which dopamine release events were suppressed did not correlate with the amplitude of white noise; thereby leading them to conclude that transient dopamine signals in the core region of the nucleus accumbens respond to aversive stimuli, but do not necessarily encode the value of punishment. However, there remain several unresolved issues and points of contention regarding the interpretation of the authors' results. Of note, they did not measure dopamine release during punished behavior, but rather in the presence of an aversive stimulus that increased the behavior being assessed. In addition, it is not clear whether the rats were able to discriminate between the tightly dispersed decibels of white noise presented during the Pavlovian task in which dopamine concentration was measured. While the current results are intriguing and a technical advance over preceding electrochemical studies, the overall picture of how transient dopamine signals throughout the mesocorticolimbic pathway encode aversive stimuli still requires further clarification that the current group of authors are capable of providing.

The submission includes an excellent set of well-considered experiments; I am both impressed and intrigued. However, I do have some constructive criticism, suggestions, and alternative interpretations to consider.

A timeline or illustration of the different subgroups and conditions under which FSCV recordings occurred would increase the readability of the manuscript.

If the authors do not believe they are measuring dopamine (DA) value signals associated with aversive stimuli, have they considered whether they are measuring a correlate of the acoustic startle response? Acoustic startle is commonly associated with an increase in ambulation (as reported in the current manuscript). This alternative interpretation would provide an important missing piece of data from previously hypothesized neural circuitry underlying acoustic startle (see figure 6 of Koch and Schnitzler, 1997). Furthermore, the transient accumbal DA signal has previously been associated with pre-attentive sensory perception of salience. Might your results align more with Redgrave's work demonstrating that there are indeed distinct DA sensory responses that are dissociable from accumbal value signals; possibly also involved in the acoustic startle response?

Koch M, Schnitzler HU. The acoustic startle response in rats-circuits mediating evocation, inhibition and potentiation. Behavioural brain research. 1997 Dec 1;89(1-2):35-49.

The authors should discuss the current results in the context their previous work (specifically DA correlates with 22Kh USVs) with the Wohr lab, which was surprisingly not referenced in the current manuscript.

Willuhn I, Tose A, Wanat MJ, Hart AS, Hollon NG, Phillips PE, Schwarting RK, Wöhr M. Phasic dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens in response to pro-social 50 kHz ultrasonic vocalizations in rats. Journal of Neuroscience. 2014 Aug 6;34(32):10616-23.

It is not clear whether rats could actually discriminate between the different tightly dispersed white noise volumes in the Pavlovian task during FSCV measurements-a centrally important experiment to support the authors' conclusions about dopamine and value. Based on my current interpretation of the methods, rats were able to discriminate between the white noise volumes in the operant choice task, but the conditions were substantially different from those in which the FSCV recordings occurred. Aside from being instrumental rather than Pavlovian, five consecutive training sessions occurred for each of three white noise volumes (70, 90, 96db) before discrimination testing was tested; and approximately 100 trials occurred in each session, with a single white noise volume being tested per session. Then, during volume-response FSCV recordings, each of four white noise volumes (70, 80, 90, 96db) were randomly played 12 times each in a single session. In a separate group of recordings, the authors performed FSCV recordings in the presence of 80 vs. 96db white noise volumes. Compared to the volume-response FSCV recordings, more training and trials occurred but, the Pavlovian trials were still randomly presented within a session. Thus, I caution against assuming that the animals could discriminate between the less dispersed and randomly presented white noise volumes presented in the single session Pavlovian experiments (particularly those depicted in 2E) based on the results from a methodologically distinct instrumental choice experiment. The authors should further address (either experimentally or logically) why the reader should accept that the rats could discriminate between the tightly spaced decibel volumes (particularly in the volume-response experiment).

Please provide additional clarification on figure 2B and your interpretations of it. First, the dopamine response to the CS predicting the aversive stimulus does seem to increase with experience (albeit quickly), which I contend contradicts your statement starting on line 293: 'Although the WN-predictive, conditioned cue acquired the ability to reliably suppress NAC dopamine release, no substantial transfer of this effect from US to CS occurred a prerequisite for a prediction error signal.' Aversive stimuli are known to rapidly induce conditioned responses. For example, a conditioned fear response is often established in a single fear conditioning session with just a few pairings of the CS and aversive stimuli. Thus, I contend (as the authors generally indicate in the results) that the US to CS transfer does indeed occur during aversive conditioning, it just occurred rapidly (on day 1; as would occur in standard fear conditioning). Similar to the presentation of extinction data in 2A, what do the CS and US data look like trial-by-trial on day 1 of aversive conditioning?

Please provide an explanation regarding the degrees of freedom associated with the statistics used for your comparisons in figure 2B (lines 242-244). It is unclear to me how the data points from the top figures transfer to the bottom figures and the degrees of freedom are adding to my confusion.

Also, what affect did smoothing the data with a 10-point median filter prior to analysis have on the results? While smoothing the data for visual presentation is common, I question whether performing statistical analysis on the data after smoothing it might affect the results?

Furthermore, the maximal amplitude of the CS associated DA response during appetitive conditioning appears to be comparable between day 1 and day 6 in the top right panel of 2B. Thus, it seems that the duration of the signal, rather than it's amplitude, is responsible for the significant effect shown in the bar graph of the bottom panel of 2B. From this observation, is the duration of the signal not accounting for the majority of appetitive value coding? Did smoothing the data contribute to the longer duration?

The authors found that a longer duration of white-noise exposure produced a longer suppression in dopamine release. One could argue that both the frequency and amplitude of a signal should influence neural coding. Thus, why would a prolonged reduction in frequency not be reflective of greater aversive value? Why do the authors exclusively consider the amplitude of their dopamine in the context of aversive value determinations?

The use of white noise as an aversive stimulus is championed by the authors because it does not produce the behavioral confound of freezing observed in standard fear conditioning approaches using electrical footshock. However, white noise and its conditioned predictor increased ambulatory behavior in the current study. Thus, how is the logic of avoiding behavioral DA responses not flawed? Could DA responses correlate to the initiation of action (which could be dissociable from speed) not confound DA value coding assessments across different volumes of white noise?

I also have some related critiques to consider regarding the benefits of white noise espoused in the discussion, starting on line 435. I already pointed out that the logic of using white noise because it doesn't induce freezing and thereby avoids movement-DA related confounds is flawed as white noise increased ambulation-which again could confound DA value coding of aversive stimuli if indeed DA transients are directly related to movement. But the data from the current study and others (PMID: 24345819, figure 2) might suggest that accumbal transients are not actually correlated in a positive way to general increases in activity. Regardless, I also take issue with point 2 and 3 (line 438) because foot shock can also maintain avoidance across many trials and sessions and be titrated with varying valence and contingencies; what are you contrasting white noise too? Point 4 does not remove the potential confound of Redgrave's work, as he has repeatedly demonstrated that the accumbal transient DA response can be induced by 'pre-attentive' subcortical sensory input. Point 6 is also not exactly accurate as properly isolating the electrical components of a shock generator eliminates the noise artifacts it can produce; thus, white noise might be easier but I don't think it is fair to imply that properly set-up electrical foot shock interferes with or jeopardizes FSCV recordings. It is fair that electrical artifacts are detected during single-unit recordings but they are easy to detect and remove during sorting.

The study would be strengthened by a core vs. shell vs. PFC comparison but at the very least, the literature regarding the role of dopamine in these distinct regions should be addressed in the discussion. I acknowledge that performing measurements of DA release in the PFC is a fraught endeavor but, at this level of journal I would expect that you at least address the Tye lab's data on aversive stimuli and the PFC (generally reviewed in: Vander Weele et al. 2019). Is it possible that DA signals in the PFC but not the NAc core encode aversive value? You also point out that Badrinarayan et al., 2012 reported that the same CS that reduced dopamine in the core increased DA in the shell-a somewhat paradoxical finding that was neither explored in the current study nor addressed in the discussion. While it is an important replication to show that NAc DA in the core is reduced by conditioned predictors of aversive stimuli, and the analysis done in figure 3 is an impressive advance over previous studies, I am left questioning the advance provided by the current data set. The primary positive effect in the core is a replication. Building a story on the general role transient dopamine signals play in encoding aversive stimuli using negative FSCV effects that were determined using tightly spaced decibels of white noise that the rat may not have been able to discriminate is shaky.

I strongly suggest that the authors not use the term punishment in the context of their results and instead use a term such as aversive stimulus. While multiple definitions of punishment exist in the literature, the one that is almost universally taught in the psychological context of animal behavior today is that of Azrin and Holz (1966), which considers punishment as a reduction in behavior in response to a stimulus. According to this definition, the behavioral response is the key element in determining whether you are observing punishment or a reinforcement; with punishment describing a decrease in behavior and reinforcement describing an increase in behavior. It is additionally worth considering that an aversive stimulus (e.g., electrical shock) can function as either a punisher or a reinforcer (i.e., something that increases behavior) in the operant context (McKearny, 1966; Morse and McKearney 1977), during imprinting (Hess, 1959), or in human interaction (Mello 1978; Sack and Miller, 1975). In the current study white noise does seem to punish food-maintained responding in one context, but also increases ambulatory behavior in another context.

Azrin NH, Holz WC. Punishment. Operant behavior: Areas of research and application. 1966:380-447

McKearney JW. Maintenance of responding under a fixed-interval schedule of electric shock-presentation. Science. 1968 Jun 14;160(3833):1249-51.

Morse WH, McKearney JW, Kelleher RT. Control of behavior by noxious stimuli. In Handbook of psychopharmacology 1977 (pp. 151-180). Springer, Boston, MA.

Hess EH. Imprinting. Science. 1959 Jul 17;130(3368):133-41.

Mello NK. Control of drug self-administration: The role of aversive consequences. Phencyclidine (PCP) Abuse: An appraisal. National Institute on Drug Abuse Research Monograph. 1978 Aug 1(21):289-308.

Sack RL, Miller W. Masochism: A clinical and theoretical overview. Psychiatry. 1975 Aug 1;38(3):244-57.

Along this same line of thought, could it not be concluded that DA might scale with the value of punishment but not of aversive stimuli that do not actually reduce the occurrence of a behavior? Punishment-associated DA signals in the basal ganglia might be more correlated to stimuli that actually reduce behavior given this neural circuit's well-determined role in goal-directed learning. Thus, if you want to conclude that DA fails to encode punishment (rather than an aversive stimulus), I would want to actually see transient DA signals failing to correlate to stimuli that reduce behavior to different magnitudes.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors did an excellent job addressing my previous concerns. Of note, their additional data provide convincing evidence that animals could discriminate the different db of white noise and that all intensities function as aversive stimuli in naive rats. The additional locomotor control experiments also strengthen the manuscript. The text is also significantly improved, particularly regarding the concept of punishment. I found the experiments to be more intriguing with better framing. The new additional summary table helped me navigate the manuscript and, importantly, illustrates the impressive breadth of experiments conducted to address a contentious and important question in the field.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have done a good job at responding to previous comments. I do think that the study is interesting and important for the field. I have a few additional comments that should be addressed.

Several manuscripts have come out recently specifically looking at dopamine release and aversive associative learning. These are surprisingly not cited or mentioned at all in the current manuscript and are highly relevant to the current work (Kutlu et al., 2022, Nature Neuroscience; Kutlu et al., 2021,. Current Biology). Both of these studies record dopamine release in the NAc core during aversive conditioning and relate dopamine signals to aversive stimulus responses and omissions based on previous predictions.

It would be interesting and important for the authors to discuss how aversive stimuli that induce different unconditioned responses – freezing, vs increased motor activity – could relate to dopamine signatures that they induce. Would the authors expect that dopamine responses to aversive stimuli that induce freezing be opposite to those that drive increases in activity?

claims.claim: In the tail of the striatum, aversive events exclusively result in increased dopaminergic activity.
claims.source: In contrast, in the tail of the striatum, aversive events exclusively result in increased dopaminergic activity (Menegas et al., 2017; Menegas et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies on the tail of the striatum.

claims.claim: Most studies observe a change in dopaminergic activity in response to aversive stimuli, with substantial differences between striatal regions.
claims.source: Overall, it can be concluded that most studies observe a change in dopaminergic activity in response to aversive stimuli, that there are substantial differences between striatal regions in this response, and that it remains unclear what determines whether aversive events provoke an increase or a decrease in dopaminergic activity within striatal regions.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from review of literature on regional dopamine responses.

claims.claim: Some studies have observed aspects of a dopamine aversive prediction error (APE), such as predictive cues adopting the dopamine response of aversive stimuli.
claims.source: other studies have observed aspects of a dopamine APE, such as the predictive cue adopting the dopamine response of an aversive stimulus (Guarraci and Kapp, 1999; Oleson et al., 2012; Badrinarayan et al., 2012), or an APE-like response when the aversive stimulus was unpredicted or omitted (Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009; Matsumoto et al., 2016; Menegas et al., 2017; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; de Jong et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing APE-like features.

claims.claim: In cases of omission or early termination of an expected aversive event, rewarding aspects of a milder-than-expected event (RPE) may be mixed with an APE.
claims.source: However, it should be kept in mind that in case of omission or early termination of an expected aversive event, rewarding aspects of a milder-than-expected aversive event (RPE) may be mixed with an APE (Oleson et al., 2012; Salinas-Hernández et al., 2018; Stelly et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about confounding factors in APE interpretation.

claims.claim: The NAC is a hotspot for reward prediction error (RPE)-like signals and is tightly linked to motivational processes related to aversion avoidance.
claims.source: Using FSCV, we measured the NAC dopamine response to these conditions since the NAC is a hotspot for RPE-like signals (Flagel et al., 2011; Papageorgiou et al., 2016) and is also tightly linked to motivational processes related to aversion avoidance (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; Stelly et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on NAC function in reward and aversion.

claims.claim: White noise (WN) possesses several merits as an aversive stimulus: it is well-tolerated, not painful, precisely controllable, aversive without inducing freezing, does not jeopardize recording equipment, does not introduce artifacts, and can be administered reliably.
claims.source: WN possesses several merits as it is well-tolerated by rats and is not painful, precisely controllable (intensity and duration can be effortlessly titrated), aversive without inducing freezing (most pertinent to this study as this might interfere with the dopamine signal), does not jeopardize the recording equipment, does not introduce artifacts to the recordings, and can be administered reliably (see 'Discussion').
claims.evidence: Based on the authors' experimental experience and rationale for stimulus choice.

claims.claim: WN at intensities not prone to cause hearing loss is moderately aversive and does not induce freezing but provokes mild behavioral activation.
claims.source: First, at intensities that are not prone to cause loss of hearing (Escabi et al., 2019), WN is moderately aversive (Campbell and Bloom, 1965; Hughes and Bardo, 1981), and as such does not induce freezing, but instead provokes mild behavioral activation.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on WN effects and hearing safety.

claims.claim: Lack of movement is often associated with diminished activity of the dopamine system, which may confound interpretation of negative dopamine signals in the context of aversive events.
claims.source: This is particularly relevant with regard to studies relating dopamine function to behavioral read-outs since lack of movement is often associated with diminished activity of the dopamine system and, thus, may confound the interpretation of negative dopamine signals in the context of aversive events.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of dopamine-movement relationships and logical inference about confounds.

claims.claim: The behavioral activation observed in response to WN might reflect an increased motivation to escape.
claims.source: The behavioral activation we observe in response to WN might reflect an increased motivation to escape, which we cannot ascertain as our task was Pavlovian (thus, without an active avoidance component: the WN was inescapable).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of behavioral observations with acknowledgment of experimental limitations.

claims.claim: During mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine may be uncoupled from its usual, more direct behavioral impact.
claims.source: Notably, the observed decline in dopamine was not at all correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis; thus, it is conceivable that during mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine was uncoupled from its usual, more direct behavioral impact.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the lack of correlation between dopamine and movement.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine does not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an aversive prediction error (APE) when aversive stimulus intensity or value is varied.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that the NAC dopamine signals we observed did not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an APE, when aversive stimulus intensity or value was varied.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from applying mathematical framework to experimental data.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration.
claims.source: In summary, we conclude that dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with varying WN durations.

claims.claim: The only evidence of an APE-like signal in the data was found after unpredicted WN.
claims.source: and the only evidence of an APE-like signal in our data was found after unpredicted WN
claims.evidence: Summary of findings regarding prediction error signals.

claims.claim: Several experimental accounts are incompatible with an APE function of NAC dopamine.
claims.source: whereas several of our other experimental accounts are incompatible with an APE function of NAC dopamine.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine encodes both reward and aversive prediction.
claims.source: Taken together, this suggests that NAC dopamine encodes both reward and aversive prediction.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from observations of dopamine responses to predictive cues.

claims.claim: Decreases in dopamine concentration do not scale with WN intensity, unlike reward processing where reward size or probability is encoded.
claims.source: However, decreases in dopamine concentration did not scale with WN intensity, unlike what is well-established for reward processing, where reward size or probability is encoded both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli (Gan et al., 2010; Tobler et al., 2005; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Comparison of current findings with established literature on reward encoding.

claims.claim: The diminishing effect of WN on NAC dopamine may be related to pre-attentive processes involved in saliency and novelty, dissociable from NAC value signals.
claims.source: Thus, one could speculate that the diminishing effect of WN on NAC dopamine may be related to pre-attentive processes involved in saliency and novelty – dissociable from NAC value signals (Redgrave and Gurney, 2006; Kutlu et al., 2021; Kutlu et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine does not encode aversive and appetitive stimuli (and their prediction) in the same way.
claims.source: Thus, NAC dopamine does not encode aversive and appetitive stimuli (and their prediction) in the same way.
claims.evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison of aversive and appetitive conditioning data.

claims.claim: The basic nature of aversion-related dopamine signals is different from that of rewards, with larger and faster changes for rewards compared to aversive events.
claims.source: Moreover, the basic nature of aversion-related dopamine signals in our data was different from that of rewards. For example, the temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the respective reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning. Another example is that reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of temporal and magnitude characteristics between reward and aversion signals.

claims.claim: The dopamine system has a bigger dynamic range for increasing activity compared to decreasing activity, which may be a structurally limiting factor on what can be encoded by dopamine reduction.
claims.source: More specifically, the dopamine system presumably has a bigger dynamic range for increasing activity; it can do so, for example, by increasing the number of cells firing and their firing frequency (and thereby the total number of dopamine-containing vesicles being released). In contrast, dopamine-signaling reduction cannot drop below a certain point since the cells' maximum response is to cease firing altogether and extracellular dopamine can only be removed relatively slowly or must diffuse away. This disparity could translate into a structurally limiting factor on what can be encoded by a reduction in dopamine concentration and explain some of the abovementioned differences in function.
claims.evidence: Speculative mechanistic explanation based on known physiology of dopamine neurons.

claims.claim: The slow-ramping declining and recovery slopes observed do not reflect system limits, as evidenced by steeper changes in other conditions.
claims.source: However, the slow-ramping declining and recovery slopes we observed do not reflect the system limits since the very first exposure to WN resulted in a steeper decline and rewards given during WN resulted in steeper increases.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of dopamine dynamics across different experimental conditions.

claims.claim: Aversive events are encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that there are a few similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, but overall we found more differences between them – hinting at aversive events being encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
claims.evidence: Summary interpretation of findings comparing reward and aversion encoding.

claims.claim: WN is a valuable and versatile aversive stimulus well-suited to probe how the brain processes aversive stimuli.
claims.source: In summary, our findings demonstrate that WN is a valuable and versatile aversive stimulus that is well-suited to probe how the brain processes aversive stimuli.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion about the utility of WN as an experimental tool.

claims.claim: Dopamine tracks the anticipation and duration of an aversive event as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that dopamine tracks the anticipation and duration of an aversive event. This tracking materializes as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus (even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration).
claims.evidence: Summary of findings on temporal dynamics of dopamine during aversive events.

claims.claim: Slowly ramping aversion signals may play an anticipatory role for certain defensive behaviors since animals were behaviorally activated during the aversive event.
claims.source: Such aversion tracking may play an anticipatory role for certain defensive behaviors since the animals were behaviorally activated during the aversive event.
claims.evidence: Speculative functional interpretation based on observed behavioral activation.

claims.claim: Slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal rather than a quantitative or scalar APE signal.
claims.source: Furthermore, we speculate that these slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal (other than a quantitative or scalar APE signal) since the unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation based on differential response to unpredicted WN.

claims.claim: Dopamine tracks both positive and negative valence in their temporal aspects and prediction, but exact value and error is only encoded for rewards in the upward direction of NAC dopamine concentration.
claims.source: Thus, we conclude that dopamine tracks both positive and negative valence in their temporal aspects and prediction, but that quantitatively speaking, the exact value and error is only encoded for rewards, in the upward direction of NAC dopamine concentration.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion integrating findings on reward and aversion encoding.

claims.claim: Aversive value and aversive prediction errors (APEs) are encoded in other brain regions, not in NAC dopamine.
claims.source: This implies that aversive value and APEs are encoded in other brain regions.
claims.evidence: Inference drawn from the lack of APE encoding in NAC dopamine.

claims.claim: Increased locomotion speed associated with decreased dopamine release during WN exposure represents a rare relationship between dopamine and behavior.
claims.source: Interestingly, the use of WN revealed a rare relationship between dopamine and behavior: increased locomotion speed was associated with a decrease in dopamine release.
claims.evidence: Based on observed dissociation between typical dopamine-behavior relationships.

claims.claim: Behavioral activation is usually associated with increased dopamine signaling, while lack of movement or freezing is associated with decreased dopamine.
claims.source: Behavioral activation is usually associated with increased dopamine signaling (Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Berridge and Robinson, 1998; da Silva et al., 2018; Coddington and Dudman, 2019), whereas a lack of movement or even freezing, depending on stimulus intensity, is often associated with decreased dopamine (e.g., Oleson et al., 2012; Badrinarayan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine-behavior relationships.

claims.claim: The hypothesis that directionality of changes in dopamine concentration reflects the chosen behavioral strategy (active or passive) when confronted with aversive stimuli is not universally applicable.
claims.source: These frequently observed association patterns have prompted the hypothesis that the directionality of changes in dopamine concentration reflects the chosen behavioral strategy when confronted with aversive stimuli: an active or a passive reaction (Badrinarayan et al., 2012). Our results, however, prove that this hypothesis is not universally applicable.
claims.evidence: Based on current findings contradicting the cited hypothesis.

claims.claim: Freezing elicited via electric shocks is accompanied by decreased NAC dopamine activity.
claims.source: Freezing elicited via electric shocks is accompanied by decreased NAC dopamine activity (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Stelly et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to literature on dopamine responses to shock-induced freezing.

claims.claim: During mild WN exposure, NAC dopamine decline was not correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis.
claims.source: Notably, the observed decline in dopamine was not at all correlated with movement on a trial-by-trial basis
claims.evidence: Based on regression analysis showing no correlation.

claims.claim: Fiorillo (2013) concluded that dopamine is insensitive to aversiveness based on three criteria: no difference between aversive and neutral stimuli, no effect of prediction, and no integration of rewarding and aversive values.
claims.source: Their conclusions range from 'dopamine is insensitive to aversiveness' (Fiorillo, 2013), to the other extreme of 'dopamine serves as an APE' (Matsumoto et al., 2016). Fiorillo, 2013 ruled out the existence of a dopamine APE because (1) dopamine-neuron firing did not differ between presentation of aversive and neutral stimuli, (2) prediction of an aversive event did not affect firing, and (3) no integration of rewarding and aversive values was observed.
claims.evidence: Summary of conclusions from cited study.

claims.claim: Matsumoto et al. (2016) found evidence for all three requirements of an APE and concluded that dopamine neurons encode a value prediction error equally for both rewards and aversive stimuli.
claims.source: In contrast, Matsumoto et al., 2016 found evidence for all three of these requirements and, therefore, concluded that dopamine neurons are capable of encoding a value prediction error (equally for both rewards and aversive stimuli).
claims.evidence: Summary of conclusions from cited study.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between Fiorillo (2013) and Matsumoto et al. (2016) could be partially explained by recording from different brain regions (substantia nigra vs. VTA) and different species (monkeys vs. mice).
claims.source: This discrepancy could partially be explained by the fact that Matsumoto et al., 2016 recorded from dopaminergic neurons in the VTA (of mice), whereas the majority of the neurons that Fiorillo, 2013 recorded were in the substantia nigra (of monkeys).
claims.evidence: Inference about methodological differences explaining contradictory findings.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine is released from terminals that originate from neurons in the VTA.
claims.source: Since we measured extracellular concentrations of NAC dopamine, which is released from terminals that originate from neurons in the VTA (Ikemoto, 2007)
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical literature.

claims.claim: Context was irrelevant to the magnitude of dopamine response to aversive events and rewards in the current study.
claims.source: although a noteworthy contrast is that in our data, context was irrelevant to the magnitude of dopamine response to the aversive event and reward: it made no difference for the acute dopamine response magnitude whether the aversive stimulus was delivered in rewarding contexts or not.
claims.evidence: Based on experimental findings comparing different reward contexts.

claims.claim: The NAC dopamine signals observed did not fulfill the axiomatic criteria of an APE when aversive stimulus intensity or value was varied, as tested using the mathematical approach of Caplin and Dean (2007).
claims.source: Next, however, we took inspiration from Hart et al., 2014, who used a mathematical approach developed by Caplin and Dean, 2007 to confirm the encoding of RPE signals by NAC dopamine. They used a deterministic and a probabilistic choice task in order to determine whether dopamine signals fulfilled three axioms that were considered necessary for a RPE signal: 'consistent prize ordering,' 'consistent lottery ordering,' and 'no surprise equivalence.' We employed the abovementioned deterministic and probabilistic Pavlovian conditioning tasks to identify an APE, instead of an RPE, by exposing rats to low- and high-dB WN, predicted by two different tones, with either a 100% probability (deterministic task) or with different probabilities (probabilistic task).
claims.evidence: Based on application of mathematical framework to experimental data.

claims.claim: The third axiom (no surprise equivalence) was fulfilled since no differences in dopamine were observed during the WN epoch in the deterministic task.
claims.source: We did not observe differences in dopamine concentration during the WN epoch in the deterministic task, which fulfills the third axiom (no surprise equivalence), since the prediction error is zero for both of these conditions.
claims.evidence: Based on analysis of deterministic task data in relation to axiomatic criteria.

claims.claim: The first two axioms (consistent prize ordering and consistent lottery ordering) were not fulfilled since no differences in dopamine were detected when different WN intensities were presented with different probabilities.
claims.source: But the first two axioms were not fulfilled since we did not detect differences in dopamine during the WN epoch, when different WN intensities were presented with different probabilities.
claims.evidence: Based on analysis of probabilistic task data in relation to axiomatic criteria.

claims.claim: Rats avoided higher-dB WN more than lower-dB WN and exhibited WN dB-dependent locomotor activation, indicating that WN aversiveness scales with intensity and rats can discriminate between intensities.
claims.source: Rats avoided higher-dB WN more than lower-dB WN (Figure 1B) and exhibited WN dB-dependent locomotor activation (Figure 2F), indicating that WN aversiveness scales with WN intensity and that rats are able to discriminate between different WN intensities.
claims.evidence: Based on behavioral data from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration, as evidenced by continuation of declining dopamine slope during extended WN and prompt cessation at WN offset.
claims.source: Extended WN elicited a continuation of the same declining dopamine concentration slope, which ceased promptly at WN cessation, after which dopamine slowly ramped backup toward baseline with a reversed, inclining slope. Thus, although the signal reflected the duration of extended WN, no discernible error component was evident.
claims.evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during extended WN trials.

claims.claim: When WN was omitted, no error signal was observed; instead, the dopamine signal slowly returned to baseline levels.
claims.source: When WN was omitted, we did not observe an error signal either: instead, again, the signal slowly returned to baseline levels.
claims.evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during WN omission trials.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine signals more than simply tracking the presence of aversive stimuli, as evidenced by the differential recovery slope after unpredicted WN.
claims.source: This flattened recovery slope indicates that NAC dopamine signals more than simply track the presence of aversive stimuli; in addition, it may relate to the failed anticipation of an aversive event (based on reliance on the predictive cue), and, thus, indicate altered cue-WN contingencies.
claims.evidence: Interpretation of differential recovery slope as indicating additional signaling beyond stimulus tracking.

claims.claim: NAC dopamine encodes rewarding and aversive events with opposite directionality, consistent with most literature.
claims.source: Consistent with most literature (Badrinarayan et al., 2012; Oleson et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Stelly et al., 2019), we found that NAC dopamine encodes rewarding and aversive events with opposite directionality.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of dopamine responses to rewards and aversive stimuli, supported by citations.

claims.claim: A cue predicting an aversive stimulus can adopt the ability to prompt dopamine changes the way the aversive stimulus itself would.
claims.source: Furthermore, we report that a cue predicting an aversive stimulus can adopt the ability to prompt dopamine changes the way the aversive stimulus itself would.
claims.evidence: Based on observations of conditioned dopamine responses to predictive cues.

claims.claim: Reward size or probability is encoded by dopamine both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli.
claims.source: However, decreases in dopamine concentration did not scale with WN intensity, unlike what is well-established for reward processing, where reward size or probability is encoded both for the reward itself and for predictive stimuli (Gan et al., 2010; Tobler et al., 2005; Watabe-Uchida et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on reward encoding.

claims.claim: Encoding of a prediction error is one of the best-characterized features of reward-related dopamine signaling.
claims.source: Furthermore, encoding of a prediction error, which is one of the best-characterized features of reward-related dopamine signaling, did not occur for aversive events.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of dopamine function in reward processing.

claims.claim: The temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning.
claims.source: For example, the temporal signal shift toward the earliest predictor of the respective reinforcing stimulus, as described for rewards, is incomplete for aversive conditioning.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of temporal dynamics between reward and aversive conditioning.

claims.claim: Reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
claims.source: Another example is that reward-related changes in extracellular dopamine concentration are substantially larger and faster compared to aversive events.
claims.evidence: Based on comparison of magnitude and kinetics of dopamine changes.

claims.claim: Disparate qualitative differences were found in NAC-dopamine responses to the presentation of ultrasonic vocalizations associated with rewarding and aversive events.
claims.source: Furthermore, disparate qualitative differences were also found in NAC-dopamine responses to the presentation of ultrasonic vocalizations that are associated with rewarding and aversive events (Willuhn et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study on dopamine responses to vocalizations.

claims.claim: There are more differences than similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, hinting at aversive events being encoded more rudimentarily in a qualitative fashion.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that there are a few similarities between dopamine encoding of rewards and aversive stimuli, but overall we found more differences between them – hinting at aversive events being encoded by NAC dopamine more rudimentarily in a qualitative instead of quantitative fashion.
claims.evidence: Summary interpretation of comparative findings.

claims.claim: Even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration.
claims.source: This tracking materializes as a perpetually declining dopamine ramp that progresses without altering its slope until offset of the aversive stimulus (even WN lasting for 24 s did not reach a plateau of minimal dopamine concentration).
claims.evidence: Based on FSCV measurements during prolonged WN exposure.

claims.claim: The unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus, suggesting contribution to a qualitative learning signal.
claims.source: Furthermore, we speculate that these slowly ramping aversion signals may contribute to a qualitative learning signal (other than a quantitative or scalar APE signal) since the unexpected aversive stimulus elicited a response beyond simply tracking the stimulus.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation based on differential response to unpredicted WN.

results.result: White noise (WN) is an effective aversive stimulus in rats, demonstrating dose-dependent aversiveness across multiple behavioral paradigms including place aversion, approach-avoidance foraging, and operant choice tasks. WN is more aversive than pure tones and stimulates locomotor activity in a dose-dependent manner, with rats able to discriminate between different WN intensities. The behavioral response to WN is reliable across sessions without sensitization or habituation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 collectively establish WN as a validated aversive stimulus through multiple independent behavioral assays with appropriate statistical analyses (all p<0.05). The dose-response relationships, discrimination abilities, and temporal stability are well-documented across different cohorts of animals with consistent findings.

results.result: WN exposure produces an unconditioned decrease in NAC dopamine concentration observable from the first trial, while a predictive cue acquires the ability to decrease dopamine as a conditioned response developing over trials 5-10. However, WN does not provoke a substantial temporal shift of dopamine signaling from unconditioned stimulus to conditioned cue within the first 30 trials of training.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by trial-by-trial FSCV analysis with appropriate statistical corrections (Holm-Bonferroni). The data clearly distinguish unconditioned (immediate) from conditioned (developing) responses, with significant effects documented across multiple trial blocks.

results.result: Aversive and appetitive conditioning show distinct temporal dynamics in NAC dopamine signaling. During aversive conditioning, the dopamine response shifts only partially from US to CS between day 1 and day 6, whereas appetitive conditioning shows an almost complete shift. Both conditioning types show corresponding behavioral changes (increased locomotion for aversive, increased magazine approach for appetitive).
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 are supported by mixed-effects analysis and behavioral tracking data comparing aversive (n=4) and appetitive (n=10) conditioning across days. The statistical analyses appropriately demonstrate the differential temporal dynamics, though the small sample size for aversive conditioning (n=4) is a limitation.

results.result: The conditioned dopamine response to WN-predictive cues is stable across days 5-9 and can be extinguished, with the cue losing its conditioned dopamine response over 15 extinction trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 demonstrate reliability and reversibility of the conditioned response with appropriate statistical analyses (repeated measures ANOVA, Dunn's test). The extinction data (C17) provides important evidence that the dopamine decrease is a learned association.

results.result: NAC dopamine does not encode WN intensity or aversive value. Despite behavioral evidence that rats discriminate between WN intensities (70-96 dB) and show intensity-dependent avoidance and locomotion, dopamine responses do not differ significantly across these intensities in either direct exposure or cue-prediction paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 and C92 are well-supported by multiple experiments testing different WN intensities with appropriate statistical analyses showing no significant effects (all p>0.05). The dissociation between behavioral discrimination and dopamine encoding is a key finding, though it raises questions about what neural signals do encode aversive value.

results.result: There is no correlation between locomotion speed and NAC dopamine concentration during cue and WN epochs on a trial-by-trial basis, despite WN-induced increases in locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C21 and C83 are supported by regression analyses showing very low R² values (all <0.002) and non-significant p-values (all >0.45) for both 80 dB and 96 dB WN conditions. This dissociation between dopamine and movement is important for ruling out movement-related confounds.

results.result: NAC dopamine does not fulfill the axiomatic criteria for an aversive prediction error (APE) when tested using the mathematical framework of Caplin and Dean (2007). While the third axiom (no surprise equivalence) was fulfilled, the first two axioms (consistent prize ordering and consistent lottery ordering) were not, as dopamine did not differentiate between different WN intensities presented with different probabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C22, C89-C91 apply a rigorous mathematical framework to test for APE encoding. The failure to meet 2 of 3 axiomatic criteria, despite behavioral evidence of discrimination, provides strong evidence against a full APE signal. The approach is methodologically sound, though the negative findings depend on the validity of applying reward-derived axioms to aversive stimuli.

results.result: NAC dopamine precisely tracks aversive stimulus duration but shows limited prediction error encoding. Extended WN (12s vs 6s) produces continued dopamine decline at the same rate, and omitted WN shows gradual return to baseline, neither showing clear error signals. However, unpredicted WN produces a significantly flatter recovery slope compared to predicted WN, suggesting some capacity for signaling prediction violations.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 and C93-C94 are supported by FSCV measurements with appropriate statistical corrections. The duration tracking is clear, but the interpretation of prediction error is nuanced - only unpredicted WN shows a differential signal (C28), and this is in the recovery phase rather than during the stimulus itself. This suggests a limited or qualitatively different form of prediction error encoding.

results.result: NAC dopamine integrates appetitive and aversive information in an additive manner. Reward delivery during WN produces a dopamine increase comparable to reward delivery without WN, and reward context (probability of intermittent rewards) does not affect dopamine responses to WN or its predictive cue.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32, C34, and C88 demonstrate parallel processing of reward and aversion signals with appropriate statistical comparisons. The additive integration is clearly shown, though the sample sizes are small (n=5-6). The lack of context effects is important for ruling out certain APE models.

results.result: NAC dopamine primarily tracks prediction and duration of aversive events rather than encoding a full aversive prediction error. Dopamine tracks both positive and negative valence in their temporal aspects and prediction, but quantitative value and error encoding occurs only for rewards in the upward direction of dopamine concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C33, C61-C64, and C77 represent the main conclusions synthesized from multiple experimental findings. The evidence from intensity manipulations, probabilistic tasks, duration manipulations, and comparisons with appetitive conditioning collectively support this conclusion, though some aspects (particularly the limited APE-like signal after unpredicted WN) add nuance.

results.result: The dopamine response to aversive conditioning differs qualitatively from appetitive conditioning: it is unaffected by WN value, context valence, or probabilistic contingencies; shows only partial temporal shift toward the predictive cue; and manifests as negative dopamine ramps followed by slow recovery. Unpredicted WN provokes slower post-stimulus recovery than predicted WN.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 summarize key qualitative differences between aversive and appetitive dopamine signals, supported by multiple experiments throughout the study. The characterization of the temporal profile (ramps) is well-documented in the FSCV data.

results.result: NAC dopamine encodes both reward and aversive prediction but does not encode them in the same way. Aversive-related dopamine signals differ from reward signals in magnitude (smaller), speed (slower), value encoding (absent for aversion), prediction error encoding (absent for aversion), and temporal shift dynamics (incomplete for aversion). Overall, aversive events are encoded more rudimentarily in a qualitative rather than quantitative fashion.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69, C96-C97, C100-C101, and C103 synthesize comparisons between reward and aversion encoding across multiple dimensions. The evidence is strong for qualitative differences, though the interpretation that aversion encoding is 'rudimentary' is somewhat subjective. The lack of value and error encoding for aversion is well-established by the data.

results.result: The dopamine system has a larger dynamic range for increasing activity compared to decreasing activity, which may structurally limit what can be encoded by dopamine reduction. However, the slow-ramping slopes observed do not reflect absolute system limits, as steeper changes occur in other conditions (first WN exposure, reward during WN).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 present a mechanistic hypothesis about physiological constraints on dopamine signaling. While C71 is supported by data showing steeper changes in specific conditions, C70 is largely speculative reasoning about dopamine neuron physiology. The hypothesis is plausible but not directly tested.

results.result: Dopamine tracks the anticipation and duration of aversive events as a perpetually declining ramp that continues without plateauing (even at 24s). These slowly ramping signals may play an anticipatory role for defensive behaviors and may contribute to a qualitative learning signal, as unexpected aversive stimuli elicit responses beyond simple stimulus tracking.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76, C104-C105 describe the temporal dynamics and speculate on functional significance. The duration tracking without plateau (C104) is directly supported by data. The functional interpretations (C75-C76, C105) are more speculative but reasonable given the behavioral activation observed and the differential response to unpredicted WN.

results.result: Aversive value and aversive prediction errors (APEs) are encoded in other brain regions, not in NAC dopamine.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is a logical inference from the demonstrated lack of value and full APE encoding in NAC dopamine, combined with behavioral evidence that rats do process these features. However, this is an inference about what must be happening elsewhere rather than direct evidence from other regions.

results.result: WN reveals a rare dissociation between dopamine and behavior: increased locomotion is associated with decreased dopamine release, contrary to the usual pattern where behavioral activation associates with increased dopamine. This challenges the hypothesis that dopamine directionality reflects active versus passive behavioral strategies in response to aversive stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 identify an important dissociation supported by the data (increased locomotion with decreased dopamine) and appropriately contextualize it within existing literature. The challenge to the active/passive hypothesis is valid, though the authors acknowledge this may be specific to mild, non-freezing aversive stimuli.

results.result: White noise is a valuable and versatile aversive stimulus well-suited for probing brain processing of aversive stimuli, possessing multiple experimental advantages including precise controllability, moderate aversiveness without inducing freezing, compatibility with recording equipment, and reliability across sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C73 describe the methodological advantages of WN as an experimental tool. These are supported by the authors' experimental experience, literature citations on WN effects and hearing safety, and the demonstrated reliability across the current experiments. This represents an important methodological contribution.

results.result: Lack of movement is often associated with diminished dopamine activity, which may confound interpretation of negative dopamine signals during aversive events. The behavioral activation observed with WN might reflect increased escape motivation, and NAC dopamine may be uncoupled from its usual behavioral impact during mild WN exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 discuss potential confounds and offer speculative interpretations. C58 is supported by literature citations about dopamine-movement relationships. C59 and C60 are explicitly speculative, acknowledging limitations of the Pavlovian (inescapable) design and the lack of correlation between dopamine and movement.

results.result: The diminishing effect of WN on NAC dopamine may be related to pre-attentive processes involved in saliency and novelty, dissociable from NAC value signals.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is explicitly speculative ('one could speculate') and offers an alternative interpretation for why dopamine doesn't encode WN intensity. While supported by citations to relevant literature on saliency/novelty, this hypothesis is not directly tested in the current study.

results.result: The manuscript provides an extensive review of prior literature on dopamine function in reward and aversion processing, documenting the well-established role of dopamine in reward prediction error, the inconsistent findings regarding aversive stimuli across different brain regions and measurement techniques, and the rationale for focusing on NAC dopamine.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C55 represent literature review and background knowledge, appropriately cited throughout. These establish the context and motivation for the current study, documenting both established findings (reward processing) and contradictory findings (aversion processing) that the study aims to address.

results.result: Prior studies have reached contradictory conclusions about whether dopamine encodes aversive prediction errors, ranging from 'insensitive to aversiveness' (Fiorillo 2013) to 'full APE encoding' (Matsumoto et al. 2016). These discrepancies may be partially explained by differences in recording location (substantia nigra vs VTA) and species (monkeys vs mice).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 accurately summarize key prior studies and offer reasonable explanations for contradictory findings. The authors appropriately position their NAC terminal measurements in relation to these cell body recording studies, noting that NAC receives input from VTA.

results.result: The flattened recovery slope after unpredicted WN indicates that NAC dopamine signals more than simply tracking aversive stimulus presence, potentially relating to failed anticipation and altered cue-stimulus contingencies.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 interprets the differential recovery slope (C28) as evidence for signaling beyond simple stimulus tracking. This interpretation is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat speculative about the specific information content (failed anticipation, altered contingencies).

results.result: In reward processing, dopamine encodes reward size and probability for both the reward itself and predictive stimuli, and prediction error encoding is one of the best-characterized features of reward-related dopamine signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 describe well-established features of reward-related dopamine signaling, appropriately cited to foundational literature. These serve as the comparison baseline for evaluating aversive processing.

results.result: Disparate qualitative differences were found in NAC-dopamine responses to ultrasonic vocalizations associated with rewarding versus aversive events.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 cites prior work (Willuhn et al. 2014b) showing qualitative differences in dopamine responses to reward-associated versus aversion-associated vocalizations, supporting the broader conclusion about differential encoding of positive and negative valence.
